## bh-p01 (1) pervading-the-particular-states-of-moving-and-unmoving / consisting-of-consciousness / one / endless / beginningless / Bhairava-Lord / of-helpless / by-mind-become- Yours / in-heart / I-venerate

gate: PASS · model crystal-v1 · 2026-11-01 · machine-proposed, needs human review before doctrine use
Argument map · 159 words
## bh-p01 — argument map

The object is fixed in full: all-pervading (vyāpta) particular of moving-and-unmoving states (carācarabhāvaviśeṣa), consisting of consciousness (cinmaya), one (eka), endless (ananta), beginningless (anādi). The act follows: Bhairava-Lord (bhairavanātham), refuge of the helpless (anāthaśaraṇyaṃ), venerated by mind-become-Yours (tvanmayacittatayā), in heart (hṛdi) — vande (I venerate). Veneration is not ritual offering but mental absorption: the devotee's mind becoming His (tvanmaya). The name Bhairava performs its own nirukta here: bearing/supporting the universe, the Roar (rava) of AHAM, benefactor of the terrified — all three senses lived in the single act of absorption (Tantrāloka 1.95-100). Total surrender is sized to its object: the all-pervading consciousness is venerated by absorption into it, not by offering to it.

### Open
- Whether 'carācarabhāvaviśeṣa' means particular states or the particularity of states is unresolved.
- Whether 'anādi' negates temporal beginning only or all limitation is unresolved.
- The nirukta is performed, not stated; the verse does not gloss its own name.
source →
C1 commentary · 212 words
**SUMMARY.** The devotee opens the Bhairavastava by bowing to Bhairava as the refuge of the helpless, with a mind that has already become His. The bowing is not a request but a recognition — the transformation (tvanmaya) is complete before the hymn begins. **FUNCTION.** Establishes the devotional posture that governs the entire stotra: total surrender, achieved state, no petition. **KEY TERMS.** tvanmaya (made of You) · anāthaśaraṇya (refuge of the helpless) · hṛdi (in heart) · vande (I venerate/bow). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 1 of 10. Sets the ontological ground (mind already His) that makes the subsequent claims (fearlessness, bliss, nondifference) intelligible as consequences rather than requests. **EXPLANATION.** The verse inverts the expected structure of a stotra: instead of "I bow so that You may X," it says "I bow because You already are X to me." The locative-with-causal tvanmayacittatayā places the transformation before the action. This matters because every later claim (v5 fearlessness, v6 bliss, v7 nondifference) reads as an *elaboration* of this achieved state, not an aspiration. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: philosophical identity with Bhairava (that is v2's claim, which is BLOCKED). The distinction between tvanmaya (devotional kinship) and ahaṃ śiva (identity) is preserved. **RELATED.** v2 (ontological identity claim), v7 (nondifference through hymn), IPK 1.1 (same surrender grammar in Utpaladeva).
source →

## bh-p02 — argument map

Disclosure first: all this (etad), become of You (tvanmayam), without remainder (aśeṣam), now (idānīm) appears (bhāti) to me (mama) — by the power of Your grace (tvadanugrahaśaktyā). Then declaration: You (tvaṃ), Maheśa, always (sadaiva) my self (mamātmā); made of my own self (svātmamayaṃ), all (samastam) is mine (mama) through Him (tena). Grace is the cause of both disclosure and declaration; merit is not. Appearance, then ownership — the two-step is the pratyabhijñā structure.

### Open

- Whether 'tena' refers to grace or to Maheśa is unresolved.

C1 commentary · 220 words
**SUMMARY.** BLOCKED — no L1/L2. The Sanskrit claims constitutive identity: the devotee's self is "made of" Bhairava's self (svātmamaya), always (sadaiva), with bidirectional possession (whatever is Bhairava's is the devotee's, and vice versa). **FUNCTION.** The stotra's ontological climax — the identity claim that the devotional posture (v1) and the results (v5–v8) all presuppose. **KEY TERMS.** sadaiva (always) · mamā'tmā (my own-self) · svātmamaya (made of Your own-self) · samastam (all) · maheśa (the Great Lord). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 2 of 10. Follows the surrender (v1) and precedes the concession (suffering, v3). The identity claim is the pivot: surrender (v1) → identity (v2) → suffering acknowledged (v3) → method (v4). **EXPLANATION.** BLOCKED — requires L1 before English can be trusted. The Sanskrit claim is: the self is constitutively Bhairava's (svātmamaya), and this is perennial (sadaiva). This is not philosophical identity (aham śiva) but devotional constitutiveness — the grammar preserves subject-object even while claiming composition. The bidirectional possession (mama tena samastam) means the relationship is not one-directional devotion but mutual indwelling. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** BLOCKED — needs L1 for: (1) whether samastam means "all possessions" or "all reality"; (2) whether sadaiva is metaphysical (always the case) or epistemic (recognition is always available). **RELATED.** v1 (surrender), v7 (nondifference — the conditional version of this claim), IPK 1.1 (the same identity grammar in Utpaladeva).

## bh-p03 — argument map

Fear-talk denied: with You as Lord (nāthe) pervading (viśvagaye) own self (svātmani), therefore (tena) no talk of transmigration-fear exists (na saṃsṛtibhītikathā asti). Affliction conceded in the same breath: even though (satsvapi) hard-to-bear suffering, delusion, terror-causing karma-hosts. No-fear and full-suffering together — the concession framed by the denial, resolved within the verse, not deferred. The non-dual recognition does not deny affliction; it denies fear of it: suffering is real, fear of it is not, because there is no 'other' to fear.

### Open
- Whether 'prāyeṇa' (mostly) softens the claim or qualifies it is unresolved.
- Whether 'karmagaṇa' means masses of karma or hosts of karmic beings is unresolved.

C1 commentary · 262 words
**SUMMARY.** The devotee acknowledges suffering, delusion, and terror-causing karma as present — and does not flinch. Suffering is not denied; it is held within the devotional relationship established in v1. **FUNCTION.** Prevents the stotra from reading as wish-fulfillment. Grounds devotion in realism about pain. **KEY TERMS.** duḥkha (suffering) · moha (delusion) · karmapiśāca (karma-ghosts) · satsvapi (even though present). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 3 of 10. Follows v1 (surrender) and v2 (identity, BLOCKED). Establishes the concession that makes v5 (fearlessness) meaningful — you cannot be fearless about something you don't acknowledge. **EXPLANATION.** The particle satsvapi ("even though present") does the whole work: it concedes the reality of the conditions (duḥkha, moha, bhaya) without qualifying them. The devotee's non-flinching is implied, not stated — the verse lists what is present and stops. This is the stotra's epistemology: suffering is real, and the devotee's stance toward it is unflinching rather than denying. It is not māyā-philosophy (suffering is illusion) but śūnyatā-adjacent realism (suffering is present, and the response is not aversion). **Dyczkowski lecture.** Dyczkowski reads v3 against the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: the self alone, afraid, realizes "no second" and fear disappears. The stotra's non-flinching operates on the same insight — fear from duality, dissolved from nonduality. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: that suffering ends, that it is illusory, or that the devotee is insensitive to it. The three conditions (duḥkha, moha, karmapiśāca) are listed without causal connectives — whether they form a sequence or a simultaneous set is unresolved. **RELATED.** v5 (fearlessness — the consequence of non-flinching), v10 (cosmic heat pacified — the same conditions, universalized).

C1 commentary · 222 words
**SUMMARY.** Service to Śaṅkara and firm contemplation produce a state in which the devotee's substance becomes terrifying Bhairava-power. The two practices are concurrent (not sequential) and the result is a change of nature (-maya), not a grant of capability. **FUNCTION.** Names the method: how transformation happens. Establishes sevanā + cintanā as the operative practices. **KEY TERMS.** sevanā (service) · cintanā (contemplation) · dhīra (firm/steady) · bhīṣaṇabhairavaśaktimaya (made of terrifying Bhairava-power) · -maya (suffix: composed of). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 4 of 10. After the concession (v3: suffering present), v4 names the method that produces the state claimed in v5 (fearlessness) and v6 (bliss). **EXPLANATION.** The two instrumentals — śaṅkarasevanā (by Śaṅkara-service) and cintanādhīra (in contemplation-firm) — are grammatically concurrent: they describe the devotee's condition, not a sequence. The result is bhīṣaṇabhairavaśaktimaya: the devotee becomes -maya ("made of") power. This is not siddhi (acquired power) but svabhāva (nature transformation) — the substance of the devotee changes, not the devotee's inventory of abilities. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: that the devotee gains Bhairava's powers or becomes Bhairava. The -maya suffix claims composition ("made of power"), not identity ("is Bhairava"). The causal structure (does sevanā produce cintanā, or do both independently produce the result?) is grammatically ambiguous. **RELATED.** v1 (the achieved-state reading of tvanmaya), v6 (bliss through fullness), Lakshmanjoo's teaching on bhairava-śakti as nature not attribute.

## bh-p05 — argument map

Great darkness already dispelled (dārita bhūri tamisra) by rays (dīdhiti) of awareness (saṃvid) consisting of world-becoming (bhavanmaya). C1 commentary · 295 words
**SUMMARY.** Salutation to the Lord removes all fear of death. The devotee names four mortal threats — death, Yama, the ender, karma-ghosts — and claims categorical fearlessness (na jātu bibhemi, "never at all do I fear") through namas alone. **FUNCTION.** The efficacy claim: devotion (namas) works against the ultimate threat (mortality). Makes explicit what v1 (surrender) and v3 (non-flinching) imply. **KEY TERMS.** namas (salutation/submission) · mṛtyu (death) · Yama (lord of death) · antaka (the ender) · karmapiśāca (karma-ghosts) · na jātu bibhemi (never at all I fear). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 5 of 10. The consequence of v4 (method → power): power manifests as fearlessness against the full spectrum of death. **EXPLANATION.** The four threats are not decorative — they cover mortality exhaustively: mṛtyu (the event), Yama (the administrator), antaka (the agent), karmapiśāca (the karmic residue). The verb's absolute force (na jātu = "never at all") makes this categorical, not probabilistic. Critically, the verse claims fearlessness (na bibhemi), not immortality (na mriye). The distinction matters: the devotee will still die, but will not fear dying. This is the Trika soteriology of jīvanmukta applied to its most concrete case. **Dyczkowski lecture.** Dyczkowski cautions: "freedom from fear, BUT IT TAKES TIME" — mind free of thought comes first, fearlessness develops. The verse states the destination, not the starting point. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: that the devotee survives death, or that namas produces liberation (mokṣa). The four threats may be four names for one thing (death's aspects) or four distinct entities — the verse lists them as separate accusatives, but tradition often collapses them. Whether "never at all" is current-state or permanent is unresolved. **RELATED.** v3 (suffering acknowledged — the concession that makes fearlessness meaningful), v10 (cosmic heat pacified — the same mortality, universalized), Tantrāloka 1 (jīvanmukti).
source →

C1 commentary · 225 words
**SUMMARY.** In being-full in the Lord, the self enters bliss (nirvṛti). The condition is pūrṇatā (fullness) in bhāva (the Lord's state); the result is entry (emi, "I enter") into a state the self was not already in. **FUNCTION.** The result of v4 (method) and v6 (nondifference): bliss as entered, not discovered. Names nirvṛti as the stotra's central soteriological term. **KEY TERMS.** nirvṛti (entering-without-movement / bliss) · pūrṇatā (fullness) · bhāva (state/being) · ātmani asmātman (in my self) · emi (I go/enter). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 6 of 10. The first result-claim after the method (v4) and fearlessness (v5): bliss enters through fullness. **EXPLANATION.** The verb emi (go/enter) is movement, not stasis — the self enters a state, it does not discover one it already occupies. The condition is pūrṇatā in bhāva (the Lord's being-full), which links back to v1 (mind already His) and v4 (substance made of power). The compound asmātman ("my self") keeps the subject devotional — this is not the universal ātman entering the universal Ānanda, but the devotee's self entering bliss through fullness-in-You. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: that nirvṛti = mokṣa, kaivalya, or any named liberation state. The grammatical ambiguity between "in my self" (devotional) and "in the Self" (universal) is preserved — both levels are operative in Trika. **RELATED.** v1 (achieved-state), v7 (nondifference through hymn), v4 (the method that produces pūrṇatā).

C1 commentary · 261 words
**SUMMARY.** The devotee's nondifference with Bhairava arises "then alone" (tadaiva) — when the hymn's supreme-nectar rain rises. The hymn performs nondifference: it does not describe it but is the condition under which it manifests. **FUNCTION.** The stotra becomes self-referential: the hymn itself is named as the instrument of its own claim. The devotional act and its result are the same movement. **KEY TERMS.** tadaiva (then alone) · tvadabheda (nondifference with You) · stotraparāmṛtavṛṣṭi (supreme-nectar rain of the hymn) · udeti (arises). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 7 of 10. After fearlessness (v5) and bliss (v6), v7 names the mechanism: the hymn is not praise-ornament but ontological instrument. **EXPLANATION.** "Then alone" (tadaiva) makes nondifference conditional on the hymn — it is not a permanent metaphysical doctrine but a state that manifests through stotra. The hymn-rain metaphor gives the stotra substance (it falls, it nourishes) rather than mere description. This is bhakti-advaya: nondifference achieved through devotion, not through jñāna or philosophy. The present tense of udeti suggests the rain is continuous — the condition is ongoing, not one-time. **Dyczkowski lecture.** Dyczkowski reveals the mechanism: affliction (kleśa) TRIGGERS grace — "the minute the body of troubles is filled, rain of nectar springs." Trouble and nectar are one movement, not sequential. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: universal metaphysical nonduality (advaya in the philosophical sense). The nondifference is bhakti's (devotee–Lord), conditional on the hymn. Whether it persists beyond the hymn's arising is unresolved by the verse. **RELATED.** v1 (surrender — the precondition), v8 (scripture contemplation — a parallel instrument), IPVV's reading of vimarśa as the hymn's own nature.

C1 commentary · 248 words
**SUMMARY.** Contemplation (cintā) of the Lord's scripture flows as the bliss-stream in the mind. Scripture is not studied (adhyayana) but contemplated (cintā); the result flows (syandati) rather than being produced. **FUNCTION.** Names a second instrument parallel to v7's hymn: scripture-contemplation produces the same bliss-stream. **KEY TERMS.** śāstra (scripture) · tāvaka (Your/yours) · parāmṛta (supreme nectar) · cintā (contemplation, not study) · syandati (flows) · nirvṛtidhārā (bliss-stream). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 8 of 10. The second instrument (scripture-contemplation) alongside v7's hymn: both produce bliss, one through praise, one through contemplation. **EXPLANATION.** The possessive tāvaka ("Your scripture") makes the scripture Bhairava's own — it is not an external text but His expression. The verb syandati (flows, from a spring) is deliberately non-agential: the bliss is not produced by effort but released when the channel opens. The practice named is cintā (contemplation/tasting), not adhyayana (study) — the scripture is nectar (āmṛta) to be tasted, not doctrine to be analyzed. This aligns with the Trika view that scripture reveals through resonance, not inference. **Dyczkowski lecture.** Dyczkowski clarifies: śāstra-contemplation destroys the suffering CAUSED BY vows/gifts/bathing/austerities — spiritual discipline itself is the suffering scripture replaces. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: that all scripture produces bliss, or that this is the only instrument. Which scripture "tāvaka" refers to (Āgama? Tantrāloka? the Lord's own scripture?) is unspecified. The distinction between cintā and adhyayana matters and is not flattened. **RELATED.** v7 (hymn as instrument — parallel), v6 (bliss as result), Tantrāloka's teaching on śabdarāśi and scripture as revelation.
source →

This consciousness of mine (saṃvid iyaṃ mama) dances (nṛtyati), sings (gāyati), deeply (gāḍham) rejoices (hṛṣyati) — O Bhairava-Lord. Having obtained (āpya) You, the dear (priyam): the beautiful vision alone (sudarśanam ekam), hard to get by others (durlabham anyajanaiḥ). Addressed to, and fenced to, the knower of the samaya (samayajña). Joy first, then its cause named: obtaining = vision, rare by structure.

### Open
- Whether 'samayajña' is vocative or qualifier converging on the same fence is unresolved.
- Whether 'sudarśanam ekam' means 'the one beautiful vision' or 'beautiful vision alone' is unresolved.

C1 commentary · 269 words
**SUMMARY.** BLOCKED — no L1/L2. The Sanskrit attributes four qualities to Bhairava: dear (priyam), beautiful (sudarśanam), unique (ekam), and hard-to-reach by others (durlabham anyajanaiḥ) — plus covenant-knowing (samayajñam). The devotee has access others lack, through the samaya (tantric covenant), not through merit. **FUNCTION.** Praise-verse that also makes a relational claim: the devotee's access is covenantal, not earned. Bridges the identity claim (v2) and the cosmic close (v10). **KEY TERMS.** samaya (covenant/pact) · durlabham (hard to obtain) · sudarśanam (beautiful to behold) · ekam (unique) · samayajñam (knowing the covenant). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 9 of 10. The penultimate verse: after the personal arc (v1–v8), it names why this devotee specifically has access — through samaya — before the cosmic close (v10). **EXPLANATION.** BLOCKED — requires L1. The Sanskrit attributes priya (dear), sudarśana (beautiful), eka (unique), durlabha (rare/hard-to-reach) — a set of praises. The key term samayajñam ("knowing the covenant") makes this relational: Bhairava knows the samaya (the tantric pact), and the devotee's access is through that pact, not through merit or method. This distinguishes the stotra's soteriology from karmic or jñānic frameworks: access is covenantal. **Dyczkowski lecture.** Dyczkowski: the verse describes Abhinavagupta himself (c. 997 AD). Samaya = guru-lineage covenant — Lakshmanjoo teaching this hymn on Sundays is the living samaya. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** BLOCKED — needs L1 for: (1) whether samayajñam means "covenant- knowing" (knowledge of agreement) or "time-knowing" (kāla-samaya, knowing the appointed time); (2) whether "hard to obtain by others" is factual or devotional intensification. **RELATED.** v2 (identity — the covenant's basis), v10 (the cosmic result of covenantal access), the stotra's arc from personal (v1) to cosmic (v10).

## bh-p10 — argument map

In the month of Pauṣa, on the dark tenth, Abhinavagupta made this hymn: dated, signed. By whom (yena) — devotee or hymn, undivided in effect — the pervasive (vibhuḥ), compassionate (dayāluḥ) Lord becomes (bhavati), pacifies (śamayati) the world's desert-heat of becoming — instantly (jhaṭiti). The dated hymn turns outward: private recognition cools the world. The verse moves from colophon to pacification to speed: inward dissolution (v.1) to world-pacification.

### Open
- Whether 'yena' refers to devotee or hymn is unresolved.
- Whether 'bhavamarusantāpa' is physical or existential heat is unresolved.

C1 commentary · 324 words
**SUMMARY.** The compassionate Lord instantly pacifies the world's great burning heat. This closes the stotra's arc from personal surrender (v1) to cosmic compassion (v10): the Lord's nature (dayā, compassion) produces the effect (śamana, pacification) without method or delay (jhaṭiti, in a flash). **FUNCTION.** Cosmic close. Universalizes the stotra's personal claims: what was individual (fearlessness, bliss, nondifference) becomes world-pacification. **KEY TERMS.** arusantāpa (great burning heat of the world) · śamayati (pacifies/soothes) · jhaṭiti (in a flash) · dayāluḥ (compassionate) · vibhuḥ (the Lord as all-pervading). **LOCAL CONTEXT.** Verse 10 of 10. The stotra's final movement: from "I bow" (v1, personal) to "the world's heat is pacified" (cosmic). Each verse has expanded the scope: personal surrender → personal fearlessness → personal bliss → personal nondifference → cosmic compassion. **EXPLANATION.** The causal agent is the Lord's nature (dayā, compassion), not the devotee's effort — this is the stotra's closing theology: pacification happens by compassion, not by method. The adverb jhaṭiti ("in a flash") is the most radical temporal claim in the text — instantaneous cosmic pacification. The tension with v3 (suffering acknowledged as present) is deliberate and unresolved: the heat is always present AND always being pacified. This is the perennial-present soteriology: the Lord is always cooling, the devotee is always being relieved — and the recognition of both is the stotra's own claim. **Dyczkowski lecture.** Dyczkowski dates the colophon: Vasura-saṃvatsara, Pauṣa, kṛṣṇadaśamī. Padyanavaka = nine verses (colophon counts 9, the opening vyāpta-verse being invocation). Tradition: cave entry with 10,000 disciples, chanting this hymn, then disappearance. **BOUNDARY / OPEN.** Not claimed: eschatological final pacification (the world will end), nor that suffering is already gone (v3 contradicts). The present tense (śamayati) and jhaṭiti suggest a stand
